analysis.one_liner: Blocks all court challenges to construction of natural gas pipelines approved before 2018.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have dismissed pending lawsuits over pre-2018 natural gas pipeline projects, was introduced by Rep. Carol Miller with 11 Republican cosponsors and never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strip courts of any power to review the permits behind natural gas pipelines that received federal approval before January 1, 2018 — including throwing out lawsuits already filed — so those projects could be finished with no legal challenge. It would also require construction to move ahead on the schedule in the original federal certificate. The bill was referred to a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee in April 2023 and nothing further ever happened.
analysis.who_benefits: Developers of natural gas pipelines holding Federal Energy Regulatory Commission certificates issued before 2018 that are still in effect. They could complete construction without any court ever reviewing the certificate or the federal and state permits needed to build, and lawsuits pending on the day of enactment would be promptly dismissed. Gas producers and utilities that want more pipeline capacity to move fuel to market would also benefit indirectly.

how_it_helps.text: Declares that covered projects — those with a FERC certificate of public convenience and necessity granted before January 1, 2018 and still in effect — 'shall be constructed expeditiously' in the location and form the certificate specifies.

Bars judicial review of the certificate and of any federal or state agency action required to finish construction, whether that action was issued before or after the bill's enactment, and orders the prompt dismissal of any lawsuit challenging those actions, including cases already pending in court.
Funneling any remaining challenge into a single narrow channel: only the D.C. Circuit could hear a claim that the law itself is invalid or that an action exceeds its scope.

analysis.who_pays: Landowners and communities along the affected pipeline routes lose the ability to challenge construction in any court, even if their cases are already filed. Environmental groups lose their main tool for forcing agencies to comply with environmental laws. Courts lose their usual role checking federal agency decisions, and the review-dismissal structure raises separation-of-powers and due-process questions. Any consumer benefit from lower energy costs is asserted in the bill's title but never demonstrated in the text.
analysis.who_pays_short: Landowners and communities near pipeline routes

drawbacks.text: The bill would dismiss lawsuits that were already pending in court on the day of enactment, taking away claims people and groups had already filed rather than only limiting future ones.

The judicial-review ban reaches beyond FERC's certificate to any federal or state administrative action needed to complete construction — so no court could check the environmental or safety permits either.

Removing all court review of major infrastructure decisions raises serious constitutional questions about separation of powers and due process; the bill attempts to contain this by giving the D.C. Circuit exclusive jurisdiction over challenges to the law itself.
The stated public benefit — lower energy costs — exists only in the bill's title; the text contains no provision or finding showing how ending court review would lower what consumers pay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real, narrow benefit: pipelines that were fully vetted and federally certificated before 2018 but stalled in litigation could finally be built, which supporters argue would move gas to market and modestly lower costs. But the bill pays for that with a blanket removal of judicial oversight — including retroactive dismissal of pending cases — affecting not just FERC's certificate but every environmental and landowner-related permit. For a targeted fix of genuinely stuck projects, a court-approval or deadline mechanism would have preserved some review; this bill offers none. The costs to landowners, environmental enforcement, and the courts' checking role outweigh the speculative consumer benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee from April 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025, never getting a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Carol Miller of West Virginia introduced the bill on March 29, 2023, with Reps. Reschenthaler and Mooney as original cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day, and on April 7, 2023 it was sent to the Subcommittee on Energy, Climate and Grid Security.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — through the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pipeline developers gained nothing, since their projects stayed tied up in the courts. Landowners and environmental plaintiffs are better off in the sense that courts kept their authority to review pipeline permits, because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Carol Miller
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill, which would end judicial review for pre-2018 pipeline projects.

for.name: 11 of 224 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat signed on.

against.name: Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Her committee received the bill, referred it to a subcommittee, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing or markup was ever held.

sides.party_line_note: All 11 cosponsors were Republicans and none of the 216 House Democrats signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: The bill would hand developers of half-built pipelines with pre-2018 federal certificates a litigation shield: pending lawsuits dismissed, all future review banned, construction ordered to proceed on schedule. Their gain comes directly from taking landowners' and communities' day in court away. The eligibility window fits long-stalled projects such as the Mountain Valley Pipeline, whose FERC certificate was issued in 2017.

More completed pipeline capacity means producers — particularly in gas-producing regions like Appalachia — can move more fuel to market. Whether consumers see lower prices is asserted but not shown in the bill.

Litigation is the main tool these groups and affected landowners have to force pipeline projects to comply with environmental and property laws; the bill would abolish that tool for covered projects and dismiss their existing cases.
